Subject: Dedicated GPU sizing for Luminary's Q4 realtime inference

Hi Hannah,

Quick intro: Luminary is launching v2.0 of our realtime summarization API in early November. We expect the product to have the following traffic profile at launch: a sustained baseline around 22,000 tokens/sec and intermittent bursts up to ~92,000 tokens/sec that last 60-120s (occurring in peak business hours). Our target SLO is p95 generation latency <= 350ms for the critical realtime path.

Can Redwood help propose a dedicated fleet plan that:
- maps model variants to expected tokens/sec per GPU,
- estimates the committed GPU count for a stable baseline and recommended burst headroom,
- recommends fallbacks/routing for quality vs latency tradeoffs, and
- calls out key assumptions (quantization, KV cache hit rate, sequence length distribution).

I've attached a short requirements spec with sample payloads and average sequence lengths. Happy to jump on a quick call if it helps.

Thanks,
Alex Dunn
Head of ML Engineering, Luminary
ops@luminary.ai

On Thu, Sep 30, 2026 at 10:05 AM, Hannah Schmitt wrote:
> Team — forwarding Luminary's ask.

Quick initial pass based on our recent benchmarks and the assumptions in their spec (avg seq len ~120 tokens, KV cache warm on repeated user sessions ~25% hit rate). Numbers below are approximate and assume our optimized runtime, continuous batching, and 8-bit quantized kernels on H100-class performance. I'll follow up with a small spreadsheet (luminary_tps_model.xlsx).

Assumed single-GPU tokens/sec (avg workload):
- 70B (8-bit quantized) on H100: ~1,050 tokens/sec per GPU, p95 latency estimate ~420ms (higher model quality, heavier KV usage)
- 13B (8-bit quantized) on H100: ~3,900 tokens/sec per GPU, p95 latency estimate ~260ms
- 7B (8-bit quantized) on H100: ~7,200 tokens/sec per GPU, p95 latency estimate ~190ms

Sizing calcs (raw, no headroom):
- For baseline 22,000 tps:
  - 70B: ceil(22000 / 1050) = 21 GPUs
  - 13B: ceil(22000 / 3900) = 6 GPUs
  - 7B: ceil(22000 / 7200) = 4 GPUs

- For burst 92,000 tps:
  - 70B: ceil(92000 / 1050) = 88 GPUs
  - 13B: ceil(92000 / 3900) = 24 GPUs
  - 7B: ceil(92000 / 7200) = 13 GPUs

Observations and immediate recommendations:
- 70B gives best quality but is expensive at burst scale (tens of racks). p95 exceeds their 350ms SLO at baseline on 70B unless we add heavy KV caching and shorter sequence lengths.
- 13B quantized hits the p95 target and is a practical mainline for latency-sensitive realtime.
- Practical hybrid: commit to a 13B fleet for baseline (covers p95) and route a small fraction of traffic to 70B for high-quality outputs or async post-process. Use hosted burst capacity (or a dedicated burst pool) for large spikes.

I'll put detailed per-GPU assumptions and a cost delta into luminary_tps_model.xlsx and propose a 40 GPU committed baseline with a 1:2 burst pool as a strawman (exact recompute after Karthik's headroom guidance).

Ben Carter
Enterprise Sales, Redwood Inference

Thanks Ben — good baseline. A few additional controls and a recommended final proposal:

Assumptions to call out explicitly for the customer test:
- Effective tps numbers above assume average 120-token sequences and warm KV cache hit rate 25%. If their real workload has longer sequences or lower cache locality, per-GPU tps will fall ~20-40%.
- Measured p95 includes network overhead; put an extra 30ms buffer for on-prem or cross-region traffic.

Headroom policy recommendations:
- Baseline commit: size for 110% of sustained baseline (22k * 1.1 = 24.2k) to avoid frequent autoscale churn.
- Burst planning: prepare for 2.0x of the expected burst (92k * 2.0 = 184k) as an operational planning envelope — this is the safety capacity to avoid saturation during sustained events.
- Financial planning headroom: 2.5x for worst-case runbook and DR exercises.

Concrete strawman (H100-class equiv):
- Commit: 40 GPUs running 13B quantized (expected aggregate ~156k tps theoretical peak; practical sustained ~120k with p95 ~260ms) — covers baseline plus modest growth and allows room for autoscale smoothing.
- Dedicated burst pool: reserve another 80 GPUs (can be on Dedicated or as reserved burst credits) to handle short peaks and progressive fallback to 7B when latency strictness is primary.
- Routing: primary 13B for realtime; fallback to 7B if latency spikes; quality-critical requests fork to 70B asynchronously.

Why this mix: committing 40 GPUs keeps the committed cost predictable and hits their p95 target for the typical profile; the burst pool reduces the need for huge upfront commit while still enabling capacity for large events.

Next steps before we send to Luminary:
- Run a short stress test with their sample payloads (we need their ingestion keys and a small test corpus).
- Produce a 1-page MOP with traffic assumptions, SLO mapping, and a cost delta for committed vs hosted burst.

Karthik Iyer
Principal Infra Solutions, Redwood Inference

Alex — thanks for the spec and the context. High level summary of our recommended approach:

- Primary recommendation: Commit to a 13B quantized fleet (we propose 40 H100-class GPUs) for realtime baseline. This configuration meets the p95 <= 350ms SLO for the workload in your spec and gives headroom for growth.
- Burst strategy: maintain a dedicated burst pool (recommended reserve of 80 GPUs) and use fallback routing to 7B for ultra-low-latency requests and async 70B for quality-heavy requests.
- Headroom policy: we recommend planning for 2.0x burst envelope operationally and 2.5x for worst-case DR planning.

Action items and next steps:
1) We need a small test corpus and temporary test keys to run a short stress test with your payloads.
